Country flags in a text column, as ISO 3166-1 codes

Source: R/emoji-flags.R
emoji_country.Rd

emoji_country() returns one row per country flag in the text, with the two-letter region code the flag spells and the region's name. A pair of regional indicators that spells no valid flag (U+1F1FD U+1F1FD is "XX") is returned too, with its glyph preserved and NA for the code, so a stray pair is visible rather than silently dropped.

Usage

emoji_country(data, text)

Arguments

data

A data frame or tibble containing a text column. Grouped data frames are accepted. The verbs that work a row at a time (adding columns, or keeping and expanding rows) carry the grouping through to their result, as dplyr::mutate() and dplyr::filter() do. The verbs that pool across rows – the counts, the co-occurrence edge lists, the time series – warn that they ignore the grouping and return one corpus-wide answer.

text

The text column to scan, supplied unquoted. Any atomic column is accepted and read as character, so a factor works and a numeric, Date or logical one simply contains no emoji. A list column – or a data-frame column – is refused rather than coerced, because coercing one deparses it and the emoji found would be in the code rather than in your data. What counts as an emoji is the same in every verb; see the Detection section of tidyEmoji for the one case that surprises people, code points that are emoji only when they carry U+FE0F.

Value

A tibble with the columns of data plus .emoji (the flag as it appears in the text), .emoji_iso2 (the two-letter code, NA for a pair that spells no flag) and .emoji_country_name. One row per flag, in reading order; rows without one are dropped. A grouped input stays grouped, as it does through emoji_tokens().

Details

A flag emoji is two regional indicator symbols, one per letter of a region code, so the code is plain arithmetic on the code points. The arithmetic accepts any pair, though, and only 259 pairs are flags in the catalogue; anything else is reported with .emoji_iso2 = NA. That includes a lone indicator, and it includes pairs that a bigger alphabet soup happened to produce: indicators pair up from the start of a run, so XUS reads as XU and a lone S, not as X and the United States, which is also how a phone displays it.

The code is the join key, not the name, because the code is what other packages take. Hand .emoji_iso2 to countrycode::countrycode(x, "iso2c", "country.name"), or join it to a map's ISO column, and a corpus of flags is a choropleth. Two things to know before you do:

  • Not every valid flag is a country. EU (European Union) and UN (United Nations) are flags but not ISO 3166-1 countries, and AC, CP, DG, EA, IC and TA are codes ISO reserves for territories it does not list as countries. A country-level tool will not map them.

  • .emoji_country_name is the Unicode (CLDR) English name, kept for reading the output, and it changes between Unicode versions: three names did between Emoji 16.0 and 18.0. Join on the code.

Subdivision flags such as Scotland's are tag sequences rather than indicator pairs; see emoji_subdivision().

See also

emoji_flag() to convert between codes and flags, emoji_subdivision() for England, Scotland and Wales.

Examples

df <- data.frame(id = 1:3,
                 text = c("go \U0001f1fa\U0001f1f8 and \U0001f1ef\U0001f1f5",
                          "no flags here",
                          "stray \U0001f1fd\U0001f1fd pair"))
emoji_country(df, text)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 5
#>      id text          .emoji .emoji_iso2 .emoji_country_name
#>   <int> <chr>         <chr>  <chr>       <chr>              
#> 1     1 go 🇺🇸 and 🇯🇵  🇺🇸     US          United States      
#> 2     1 go 🇺🇸 and 🇯🇵  🇯🇵     JP          Japan              
#> 3     3 stray 🇽🇽 pair 🇽🇽     NA          NA
